clue.text: Drink bitter — swallowing volume before time

indicators.note: the bitter-and-volume piece comes ahead of the time piece in the answer
the beer takes the volume letter down inside itself, like a gulp

parts.note: bitter is a type of English beer
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Someone downs a pint of bitter, gulping a large amount just before closing time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallowing' signals one piece going inside another, and 'before' fixes the charade's order; 'bitter' is a British pale ale, not the adjective the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Any liquid taken for refreshment, such as tea or ale, is a beverage.

clue.text: Plot by the French first minister produces uproar

parts.note: a bed is a plot in a garden, as a flower bed
la is French for the

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the word minister

explanation.surface: A scheme by France's prime minister causes chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam is a scene of noisy confusion, after London's old madhouse.

clue.text: A case of narcissism?

parts.note: read both as an instance of self-love and as a small cosmetics bag for one's looks

explanation.surface: Diagnosing a self-obsessed patient.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive pride in looks is this trait, and a vanity case carries make-up.

clue.text: A Tory leader in press appraisal

indicators.note: in places the A and leader letters inside the word for press

parts.note: to ring a doorbell is to press it

indicators.note: leader picks the first letter of the word Tory

explanation.surface: A Conservative chief featured in the newspapers' assessment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' looks like the news media but means push, as in ringing a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: A rating is an assessment or evaluation of standing or quality.

clue.text: It needs to have excellent pull

definitions.text: It needs to have excellent pull

parts.words: It needs to have excellent pull
parts.note: read as a strain in the sense of a pulling force, of high quality

explanation.surface: Something requires strong influence to succeed.
explanation.definitionFit: A strain is a pull or tension, and a fine one is of high quality.

clue.text: Easy lump sum includes security

indicators.note: the phrase Easy lump sum holds the answer within its run of letters

explanation.surface: A tidy cash payout comes with some financial safety attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' says the answer sits inside the words 'Easy lump sum', running from the end of 'Easy' into 'lump'.
explanation.definitionFit: Asylum is protection or refuge granted to someone, a form of safety.

clue.text: Least agitated's sick in exam

parts.note: the apostrophe S supplies its letter

indicators.note: in places the word for sick inside the word for exam

parts.note: a test is an exam
ill means sick

explanation.surface: The calmest student is the one who feels unwell during an examination.
explanation.definitionFit: Being calmest and most motionless, the superlative of still.

clue.text: Hilarity after ringing expression of disgust

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so the word for after goes round the exclamation

parts.note: later means after
ugh is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: Merriment follows a phone call that prompts an exclamation of revulsion.
explanation.definitionFit: Laughter is the sound of mirth and amusement.

clue.text: Deliberate tackle's first caught by referee

indicators.note: caught by means held inside the word for referee

parts.note: to mediate is to referee a dispute

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the word tackle

explanation.surface: A deliberate foul tackle is spotted by the match official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliberate' reads as an adjective on the tackle but is the verb, to think deeply.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder something carefully is to reflect on it at length.

clue.text: Party people providing present

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party or celebration
a nation is a people united by country or culture

explanation.surface: A gathering of folk provides a gift for someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift handed over, especially to charity, is a donation.

clue.text: Fifty-one pounds in cash

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
I is the Roman numeral for one
quid is British slang for pounds sterling

explanation.surface: A sum of fifty-one pounds paid in banknotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquid assets are money readily available, so liquid can mean ready money.

clue.text: Surprise host's in a broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are thrown about into a new order

parts.note: host's stands for host is, and its S is part of the letters used

explanation.surface: A show's presenter appears on air, causing amazement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' signals an anagram of HOSTS, IN and A, which rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To astonish someone is to amaze or startle them greatly.

clue.text: Ancient porkpie, for example, past its sell-by date

parts.note: ancient means old
a porkpie is a style of hat with a flat crown

explanation.surface: An elderly pork pie, of the kind eaten, has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the British pork pie (a pastry snack), but a porkpie is also a flat-crowned hat.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for something tired and outdated, no longer fresh or fashionable.

clue.text: Never odd or even, for instance

definitions.text: Never odd or even, for instance

parts.words: Never odd or even, for instance
parts.note: the phrase quoted reads identically backwards letter by letter, and is offered as an example

explanation.surface: A maths puzzle about a number that is neither odd nor even.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase that reads the same backwards as forwards; the quoted phrase is a well-known example.

clue.text: Telegraph is hard and dares to be different

indicators.note: different here asks for the letters to be arranged in a different order

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: The newspaper is tough and bold enough to stand out from the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' signals an anagram of H with DARES TO BE. Broadsheet is the large traditional newspaper format, as opposed to the smaller tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: The Daily Telegraph was long printed as a large-format newspaper of the traditional size.

clue.text: Blinking good way to stop leaks!

definitions.meaning: blinking means lighting up on and off
strips of metal sealing roof joints against rain

explanation.surface: A mildly cursed but effective way to plug drips.
explanation.definitionFit: Lights blinking are flashing; and roofers fit metal flashing to keep water out of joints.

clue.text: Weirdo taking one drug after another

parts.note: crack is a form of cocaine
pot is slang for cannabis, another drug

explanation.surface: An oddball takes one narcotic after another.
explanation.definitionFit: A crackpot is an eccentric or crazy person.

clue.text: Throw out a French bench

parts.note: un is French for a
a settle is a high-backed wooden bench

explanation.surface: Someone discards a French bench.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsettle someone is to disconcert or throw them off balance.

clue.text: An impediment to freedom of speech?

definitions.text: An impediment to freedom of speech?

parts.words: An impediment to freedom of speech?
parts.note: read not as censorship but as a throat ailment that literally stops a person talking

explanation.surface: A political worry about something blocking free expression.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflamed voice box makes a person hoarse or voiceless, physically hindering speech.

clue.text: Paradoxically down when you're on these…

definitions.text: Paradoxically down when you're on these…

parts.words: Paradoxically down when you're on these…
parts.note: being down on one's shoe tops means being broke, though stimulant pills lift you up

explanation.surface: A riddle about feeling low while on pep pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down on your uppers' is a British idiom for being poor, uppers being the tops of worn-out shoes; uppers are also stimulant drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Uppers are both stimulant drugs and the upper parts of shoes, hence the idiom for poverty.

clue.text: …in poor shape when you're out of it

definitions.text: …in poor shape when you're out of it

parts.words: …in poor shape when you're out of it
parts.note: being out of a certain state of balance means things are in disorder

explanation.surface: Continuing the riddle: unwell when stoned.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of kilter is an idiom for being out of balance or order.

clue.text: Strong nasal output ruining evening snooze, initially

definitions.text: Strong nasal output ruining evening snooze, initially

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of each of the six preceding words

explanation.surface: Loud noises from someone's nose spoil a nap after dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Snores are loud breathing noises through the nose during sleep.

clue.text: A revolutionary filling for empty sweet packet

indicators.note: the A and revolutionary piece fills the gap left in the emptied word
empty means the word sweet loses its inside letters, leaving its first and last

parts.note: Che Guevara is the crossword's stock revolutionary

explanation.surface: A rebel stuffs a hollowed-out candy wrapper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' leaves S and T, the first and last letters of 'sweet'; 'filling' puts A and CHE between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachet is a small sealed bag or packet, as of sugar or shampoo.

clue.text: Taking in a daughter by choice?

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter in genealogies
an option is a choice

explanation.surface: Bringing a girl into the family, if one chooses to.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a child in as one's own is the act of legally making them your child; 'taking in' works as a noun here.

clue.text: Charge that I'm to set down clue, finally

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
to put something is to set it down

indicators.note: finally points to the final letter of the word clue

explanation.surface: A solver complains about having to write a clue's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge someone with a fault is to attribute or ascribe it to them.

clue.text: Used a lot, it's said, by sailor as a guide

indicators.note: it's said means the preceding words are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: something used a lot is colloquially used loads
tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A much-used star helps a seaman steer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's said' turns LOADS into its sound-alike LODES.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodestar is a star used for navigation, so figuratively anything that serves as a guiding principle.

clue.text: Almost go out to see 'midnight express'

parts.note: the middle of night is its central letter
to utter is to express in words

explanation.surface: Seeing the film Midnight Express nearly drops you off to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'midnight' is the convention for the middle letter of 'night'. A candle gutters when it flickers and is about to die.
explanation.definitionFit: A candle flame that flickers low and nearly dies is said to gutter.

clue.text: Crumbles, perhaps, back under pressure

indicators.note: back means the word for being under pressure is read in reverse

parts.note: stressed means under pressure

explanation.surface: A person collapses, maybe, when the strain returns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbles' looks like a verb but is a plural noun: a crumble is a British baked fruit pudding with a crumbly topping.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit crumbles are examples of puddings served at the end of a meal.
